title: A Dyer's Tally of Weaves
author: a Nauvissa dyer, for the Name-Wife
body:
# The weaves

*Birch-bark, scratched with a nail, the knot of each family drawn small beside its count.*

---

Mor, the double hitch: eleven.

Oul, the reef with the tail tucked: nineteen. (The Ouls are free with other people's names. The peat does it to you.)

Sa, the running knot: six.

Lissa, the bittern's knot, two loops: four.

Nauve, the boatwright's splice: twenty-two, and one more since the thaw.

Moreva, Saeva, Oulea, the village knots: forty between them, nobody counting.

The Vale, no weave, a plain overhand, the way they tie their boots: nine.

*At the bottom, pressed harder:* She asked me to do this. She said she was losing track. I said who could lose track of a thing like this, and she looked at me as if I had asked her name.

title: The First Cord
author: the Name-Wife
body:
# Wound round a slate

*The cord is white with age and knotted in no weave of the Delta. The slate under it says, in a small even hand:*

---

The first was mine.

The Wenne girl had the flats-cough and I had nothing to give for it but what I had, so I gave that. It can be done. The cough went out of her that night and my name went out of me, and in the morning my mother called me *you*.

I have tried every cure in the marsh on it since. There is nothing in the marsh for it. There is only taking more, to see if one of them will do.

*Under it, newer, the hand less even:* None of them do.

title: The Name-Wife's Price
author: the Name-Wife
body:
# Hung from the ladder at Crookstilts

*A slate, written over and rubbed out and written over again. What is on it now:*

---

ANY CURE.

A NAME YOU KNOW. NOT YOURS. I DO NOT TAKE YOURS.

SAY IT ONCE, PLAIN, AT THE FOOT OF THE LADDER, AND GO HOME.

I AM HERE AT THE DARK OF THE MOON. THE REST OF THE MONTH I AM UNDER THE SOUTH SCARP. DO NOT COME THERE.

*Chalked under it by another hand, rubbed nearly out:* she took my brother for my boy's fever and I would do it again, and I cannot remember what he looked like, and I would do it again.

title: The Callers' Tide-Table
author: the Flood-Callers of the Sounding
body:
# The Tide-Table

*A board of bog-oak, scratched with the moon's quarters and a cut for every spring tide since the Callers came to the North Shore. Beside the cuts, in charcoal:*

---

First spring. The mark at the platform's lip. Aunsa says: it is coming.

Second spring. The mark a hand over the lip. We raised the first stage.

Third spring. The mark at the first girt. The bell cast. Ama says it must be rung from under. Aunsa says from above, the way bells are rung. They do not speak for a month.

Fourth spring. Aunsa gone to the stakes with her lanterns. The mark at the deck. Ama has run the rope down the shaft into the well.

*The next spring tide is circled twice. Beside it, in a different hand:* We will not need the next mark.

title: A Length of Knotted Rope
author: Ama Lissa
body:
# Wound round birch-bark

*The knots are the Heron Watch knots, the ones Tuo Lissa still ties on the bell-rope every night. The bark spells them out, in the careful hand of somebody writing for a person who cannot read knots.*

---

A loop: a boat went north. Mine.

A loop: a boat went north.

A loop.

A plain knot: nothing came down the channel.

A twist, undone: a lantern that did not burn out right. His.

A plain knot. A plain knot. A plain knot.

*At the end, not a knot but the rope frayed out, and on the bark:* Tuo, you sit at the bottom so the young know somebody is at the bottom. I am going to the bottom so he will know somebody is.

title: The Divers' Slate
author: the children of Oulea
body:
# Who touched the face

*A slate, scratched with a nail, wedged between two of the drowned courses where the children leave their clothes.*

---

PIP SA — IIII

WENNA OUL — IIIII II

TOLLO — I (cried)

MEO SA — IIIII IIIII I

*Under them, newer, in a careful hand:* The face's eyes were open today. Meo says they're always open. They are NOT always open.

*And under that, in another:* It was looking at the sea.

title: The Saltgate Watch-Book
author: the Saltgate garrison
body:
# The watch-book

*Ruled in the Guild's columns: the hour, the tide, the gates, the hand. The last page:*

---

**Ninth bell.** Flood making. Gates shut. All well. — *R. Ruddock, warden*

**Tenth bell.** Flood. Gates shut. Knocking in the race, again. Warden says driftwood. — *T. Pell*

**Eleventh bell.** Knocking in the race. It is not driftwood. Driftwood does not knock in threes. — *T. Pell*

**Twelfth bell.** Warden gone down to the windlass with the key. — *T. Pell*

**Twelfth bell.** —

*The rest of the column is water-stain. In the margin, much later, in a hand that shakes:* The gates are open. I could hear them all the way to the Hearth. — H. R.

title: The Sluice-Warden's Tally
author: Rook Ruddock, sluice-warden
body:
# Behind the loose stone

*A tally-stick notched in the Guild's way, and wrapped round it a page in a careful Tollmere hand:*

---

Acres won back from the Delta since the gates were hung, by my count and not the Guild's: four hundred and eleven.

Eel-runs the reedfolk on the Outfall have lost by the same count: all of them.

I have told the Guild. The Guild says an eel is a reedfolk matter and an acre is a Tollmere one. My brother Hal says the reedfolk will open the gates themselves one night. I say they will not have to. There is something under the sluice that knocks, at the spring tides, in threes, and it is patient, and it has been patient for eleven years.

If the gates are ever open and I am not, let them be shut by somebody who has stood on the south bank in eel-time and seen the Outfall empty. Or let them hang. I would not know, now, which.
